name: Irritability associated with autism spectrum disorder
summary: Aggression, self-injury, severe tantrums, and rapid mood changes in autistic children and adolescents. Only risperidone and aripiprazole are FDA-approved, for irritability associated with autistic disorder in youth; no medication is approved for core autism symptoms. Leucovorin (Wellcovorin) gained a March 2026 indication for cerebral folate transport deficiency with a confirmed FOLR1 variant, not for autism.
plainSummary: Some autistic children have intense outbursts, aggression, or self-harm. Two medicines are approved to calm this irritability, but no medicine is approved to treat autism itself.

approved.indication: Treatment of irritability associated with autistic disorder, including symptoms of aggression towards others, deliberate self-injuriousness, temper tantrums, and quickly changing moods.

population.ages: Children and adolescents 5 to 17 years (ages studied in the efficacy trials)

dosing.start: 0.25 mg/day if under 20 kg; 0.5 mg/day if 20 kg or more
dosing.target: After at least 4 days, 0.5 mg/day (under 20 kg) or 1 mg/day (20 kg or more); further increases of 0.25 or 0.5 mg at intervals of 2 weeks or more
dosing.notes: Once daily or split twice daily; if somnolence, give at bedtime or split. Lower doses in severe renal or hepatic impairment. Monitor weight, metabolic parameters, prolactin, and EPS.

boxedWarnings: Increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis
approved.plainSummary: An antipsychotic medicine that can reduce aggression, self-injury, and tantrums in autistic children; it often causes weight gain and needs regular check-ups.

source.label: DailyMed: Risperdal (risperidone) tablets, oral solution, M-Tab

verified.note: Label effective 5/2026 checked (indication 1.3, weight-based dosing 2.3). Drugs@FDA lists the Risperdal ODT (M-Tab) NDA as discontinued; generic risperidone ODT remains available.

approved.drugClass: Second-generation (atypical) antipsychotic; dopamine D2 partial agonist
approved.indication: Treatment of irritability associated with autistic disorder in pediatric patients 6 to 17 years.

dosing.target: Increase to 5 mg/day, then 10 or 15 mg/day if needed; adjust by up to 5 mg/day at intervals of at least 1 week
dosing.notes: Known CYP2D6 poor metabolizers: half the usual dose. Adjust for strong CYP2D6/CYP3A4 inhibitors or CYP3A4 inducers. Monitor weight, metabolic parameters, and EPS.

boxedWarnings: Increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis
Suicidal thoughts and behaviors with antidepressant drugs (children, adolescents, and young adults)
approved.plainSummary: An antipsychotic medicine taken once a day that can lessen outbursts, aggression, and self-harm in autistic children 6 and older.

verified.note: Label effective 1/2025 checked (indication, 2.4 dosing, CYP2D6 adjustment, boxed warning). Brand oral solution/Discmelt availability not confirmed; generics listed instead.

offLabel.use: Core autism symptoms or language impairment, especially with folate receptor alpha autoantibodies or suspected cerebral folate deficiency
offLabel.notes: Not FDA-approved for autism. In September 2025 FDA announced a planned label change, but the March 10, 2026 Wellcovorin approval covers only cerebral folate transport deficiency in adult and pediatric patients with a confirmed FOLR1 gene variant (FOLR1-CFTD), a very rare disorder, and is based on published case reports rather than trials; FDA stated evidence was insufficient for autism. Small RCTs (about 50–60 children each) reported gains in verbal communication or autism scores; replication is lacking. Generally well tolerated; irritability and agitation have been reported.

references.label: Frye RE et al. Folinic acid improves verbal communication in children with autism and language impairment: RCT. Mol Psychiatry 2018 (PMID 27752075)
Renard E et al. Folinic acid improves the score of autism in the EFFET RCT. Biochimie 2020 (PMID 32387472)
CNBC: FDA approves leucovorin for cerebral folate deficiency but not autism (Mar 10, 2026)

offLabel.use: Hyperactivity and inattention in autistic children (co-occurring ADHD symptoms)
offLabel.notes: Methylphenidate is approved for ADHD, not for autism-associated hyperactivity. In the RUPP crossover trial about half of children responded, a lower rate than in typical ADHD, with more adverse effects (irritability, social withdrawal, appetite loss).

references.label: RUPP Autism Network. Methylphenidate in pervasive developmental disorders with hyperactivity. Arch Gen Psychiatry 2005 (PMID 16275814)

offLabel.use: Hyperactivity and impulsivity in autistic children
offLabel.notes: An 8-week RCT in children with ASD showed reduced hyperactivity versus placebo. Drowsiness, fatigue, decreased appetite, and lower blood pressure and heart rate; taper to avoid rebound hypertension.

references.label: Scahill L et al. Extended-release guanfacine for hyperactivity in children with ASD. Am J Psychiatry 2015 (PMID 26315981)

offLabel.drugClass: Melatonin receptor agonist (dietary supplement in the US)
offLabel.notes: A pediatric prolonged-release formulation improved total sleep time in a 13-week RCT. In the US, melatonin is sold as a supplement with variable content; no US-approved pediatric melatonin product exists.

references.label: Gringras P et al. Pediatric prolonged-release melatonin for insomnia in children with ASD. JAACAP 2017 (PMID 29096777)
